findings.title: UWB: Ghost Peak Distance Reduction Attack
findings.description: The Ghost Peak attack is a physical-layer distance reduction attack targeting IEEE 802.15.4z HRP UWB ranging. An attacker positioned within RF range injects an early leading pulse into the Two-Way Ranging (TWR) exchange, causing the victim receiver to latch onto the injected pulse rather than the authentic signal, thereby reporting a measured distance significantly shorter than the true physical separation. This attack succeeds without breaking any cryptographic mechanism and was demonstrated to work against DW1000 and DW3000 chip families in published research from 2022. Affected systems include Apple AirTag-like access control implementations, automotive CCC Digital Key systems, and any RTLS deploying HRP UWB without pulse-shape authentication. The consequence is that physical access controls relying on UWB proximity can be bypassed entirely — for example, a vehicle keyless entry system can be unlocked from tens of meters away while the chip reports centimetre-level proximity.
findings.impact: An attacker can defeat UWB-based physical access controls by making the system believe a tag is centimetres away when it is actually tens of meters distant. This enables unauthorized entry through UWB-secured doors, vehicle keyless entry bypass, and circumvention of proximity-based safety interlocks. In industrial RTLS deployments, manipulated distance measurements can place personnel or assets in incorrect safety zones, potentially suppressing hazard alerts and creating life-safety risks.
findings.remediation_brief: Apply firmware patches from DecaWave/Qorvo that enable STS (Scrambled Timestamp Sequence) integrity checking in IEEE 802.15.4z SP3 mode, which hardens against early-pulse injection by cryptographically authenticating the leading edge timestamp. Require the STS mode to be enforced on all ranging sessions and reject sessions negotiated in legacy SP0 mode. Supplement ranging with additional physical sensors (e.g., NFC tap confirmation) for high-security access control scenarios. Monitor chip vendor advisories (Qorvo DW3000 series) and apply firmware updates as they are released.

findings.title: Authentication: Default Credentials Accepted
findings.description: The RTLS management console (Sewio RTLS Studio, Pozyx Creator, or equivalent) is accessible with factory-default credentials such as admin/admin, admin/sewio, or admin/pozyx. Default credentials are frequently left unchanged during deployment as operators rely on network segmentation rather than strong authentication. An unauthenticated remote attacker who can reach the management interface over the network gains full administrative control of the RTLS infrastructure, including the ability to modify anchor configurations, alter zone boundaries, extract all tracked position data, and inject false location records. This vulnerability has a trivially low attack complexity and requires no prior knowledge of the target environment beyond the platform type.
findings.impact: An attacker gains complete administrative control of the RTLS platform without any credential guessing or exploitation. This allows wholesale reconfiguration of anchor placements and zone boundaries, exfiltration of all historical and real-time position data for tracked personnel and assets, creation of backdoor accounts for persistent access, and the ability to push malicious firmware to anchors. In safety-critical environments, an attacker can silently disable geofence alerts or manipulate position data to mask unauthorized physical access.
findings.remediation_brief: Immediately change all default credentials to unique, randomly generated passwords of at least 16 characters. Implement account lockout after 5 failed login attempts and enforce MFA where the platform supports it. Restrict the management console to a dedicated administrative VLAN with access limited to specific administrator workstations via firewall ACLs. Audit all vendor-supplied accounts and disable or remove any service accounts that are not operationally required.

findings.title: IoT: Unauthenticated MQTT Broker
findings.description: The MQTT broker used by the RTLS platform accepts connections on TCP port 1883 without requiring a username or password, exposing a full publish/subscribe channel to any network-accessible client. Real-time position data for all tracked tags — including tag IDs, X/Y/Z coordinates, zone assignments, velocity vectors, and floor-plan identifiers — is streamed continuously over unauthenticated MQTT topics. An attacker who connects to the broker gains complete visibility into the physical location of every tracked person or asset in real time, enabling surveillance, operational intelligence gathering, and targeted physical attacks. Additionally, unauthenticated write access to the broker allows injection of fabricated position updates that will be consumed by downstream business applications.
findings.impact: An attacker with network access can passively monitor the real-time physical locations of every tracked person and asset without any credentials. This enables covert surveillance, pattern-of-life analysis, and identification of high-value targets. Write access to the broker allows injection of fabricated position data, triggering false safety alarms, suppressing legitimate zone-exit alerts, and manipulating business processes that depend on accurate location data such as inventory management and personnel safety systems.
findings.remediation_brief: Enable MQTT broker authentication by requiring a username and password for all client connections; configure Mosquitto or the embedded broker to reject anonymous connections. Migrate all RTLS MQTT traffic to TLS-encrypted port 8883 using certificates issued by an internal CA. Implement MQTT ACL (Access Control List) rules that restrict each client to only the topics it legitimately needs to publish or subscribe. Regularly audit active MQTT client sessions and broker configuration.

findings.title: IoT: RTLS Position Data Injection via MQTT
findings.description: When the MQTT broker lacks authentication (or when credentials are weak and obtainable), an attacker can publish arbitrary JSON position payloads to RTLS position topics, causing the RTLS engine to process and display fabricated location data as if it originated from legitimate anchors. This allows an attacker to teleport tracked tags to arbitrary zones, trigger false zone-entry or zone-exit alarms, suppress the displayed location of real tags by flooding with conflicting updates, and manipulate safety-critical zone occupancy decisions in industrial or healthcare environments. If the RTLS feeds a physical access control system or a hazardous zone safety interlock, injected positions can result in direct safety consequences.
findings.impact: An attacker can manipulate the perceived physical location of any tracked tag, causing the RTLS system to show personnel or assets in locations they are not. This can trigger false evacuation alerts, suppress legitimate zone-breach notifications, defeat geofenced access controls, and undermine safety interlocks in industrial environments. In healthcare settings, manipulated position data could cause staff to be dispatched to wrong locations during emergencies. Business processes relying on RTLS data for billing, compliance, or workflow automation can be subverted.
findings.remediation_brief: Require MQTT broker authentication and deploy publisher-side ACLs that restrict position topic publishing to anchor gateways only — no external client should be able to publish to position update topics. Implement message signature validation on the RTLS engine so that position payloads include an HMAC computed with an anchor-specific key, and reject any payload whose signature does not validate. Audit RTLS business logic for safety-critical zone enforcement and add secondary sensor confirmation before triggering safety interlocks.

findings.title: Injection: SQL Injection in RTLS Reporting Module
findings.description: The RTLS web platform contains SQL injection vulnerabilities in reporting and analytics endpoints where user-supplied parameters (date ranges, tag IDs, zone names, report filters) are interpolated directly into database queries without parameterisation or sanitisation. An authenticated attacker with low-privilege access to the reporting interface can extract the full database including historical position data, user credentials, API tokens, and configuration secrets via UNION-based or blind SQL injection. In environments where the RTLS database account has file-system privileges, the attacker may read operating system files or write web shells to achieve remote code execution on the database server.
findings.impact: An attacker can extract the entire RTLS database including historical position records of all tracked individuals, plaintext or hashed user credentials, API tokens, and system configuration. This data enables physical surveillance, credential reuse attacks against other systems, and potential remote code execution on the database server if file-system privileges are available. In regulated environments, a SQL injection breach of location data constitutes a reportable privacy incident.
findings.remediation_brief: Replace all dynamic SQL string construction with parameterised queries or prepared statements using the ORM or database driver's native placeholder syntax. Apply the principle of least privilege to the RTLS database account — it should have no FILE or SUPER privileges and should access only the RTLS schema. Deploy a web application firewall (WAF) with SQL injection detection rules as a defence-in-depth measure. Conduct a full code review of all user-facing query parameters and implement input validation that rejects unexpected characters.

findings.title: Unauthenticated Access: Unauthenticated RTLS REST API Endpoints
findings.description: Multiple REST API endpoints in the RTLS management platform are accessible without any authentication token or session cookie. Unauthenticated callers can enumerate all anchor hardware configurations (including firmware versions and network addressing), retrieve full tag inventories with their last known positions, and query zone boundary definitions and floor-plan metadata. This information directly enables further attacks by revealing the physical layout of the tracked environment, identifying anchor IPs and firmware versions susceptible to known CVEs, and confirming the topology of the UWB infrastructure prior to a targeted attack.
findings.impact: An attacker can remotely enumerate the entire RTLS infrastructure without credentials, obtaining anchor network addresses and firmware versions for targeted exploitation, full tag inventories revealing what is being tracked, zone boundary definitions that expose the physical security layout, and floor-plan metadata that maps the facility. This reconnaissance data significantly lowers the barrier for follow-on attacks against both the RTLS system and the physical environment it protects.
findings.remediation_brief: Implement authentication middleware that enforces a valid API token or session token on all REST API routes; return HTTP 401 for any unauthenticated request. Apply role-based access control so that read-only API tokens cannot invoke configuration-modifying endpoints. Audit the full API surface using OpenAPI/Swagger documentation against the actual route handlers to identify any routes that bypass the authentication middleware. Ensure the API is not exposed to untrusted network segments.

findings.title: UWB: UWB STS Key Weakness
findings.description: The Scrambled Timestamp Sequence (STS) used by IEEE 802.15.4z HRP UWB to authenticate ranging frames is derived from a session-level key that may be poorly seeded, statically configured, or exposed via the RTLS management API. When the STS key derivation is weak — for example, using a predictable seed derived from the tag EUI-64 or a static factory-provisioned value — an attacker who captures sufficient ranging exchanges can recover the STS key and forge authenticated ranging responses, making the distance-reduction attack resilient even against platforms that believe STS provides full protection. This finding applies to firmware versions that implement STS key management outside the secure element, or that expose STS configuration parameters over the RTLS API.
findings.impact: An attacker who recovers STS key material can forge authenticated UWB ranging frames, completely defeating the primary cryptographic defence against distance-reduction and frame-injection attacks. This means STS-protected deployments that believe they are hardened against Ghost Peak and similar attacks remain vulnerable. The attacker can manipulate ranging measurements with the same effectiveness as against unprotected SP0 mode, undermining all proximity-based access controls and safety interlocks that rely on STS for integrity.
findings.remediation_brief: Ensure STS keys are derived from a cryptographically random 128-bit seed generated inside a hardware secure element and never exposed via any management API or diagnostic interface. Rotate STS session keys per-ranging-session using a cryptographically strong key derivation function (e.g., HKDF-SHA256) with a fresh nonce. Audit RTLS API responses to confirm that no STS key material, seed values, or counter states are returned. Apply firmware updates from the chip vendor that implement IEEE 802.15.4z STS key management in the secure enclave.

findings.title: UWB: Cleartext UWB Ranging Exchange
findings.description: UWB ranging frames (Poll, Response, Final) are transmitted in IEEE 802.15.4z SP0 mode without STS or payload encryption, making the full ranging exchange observable to any attacker with appropriate RF hardware within range. Captured frames reveal tag and anchor EUI-64 addresses, sequence numbers, timing fields, and any application payload appended to the ranging frame. This exposure enables an attacker to map the UWB topology, identify specific tags of interest (such as those carried by executive personnel or used for vehicle access), build a model of normal ranging behaviour for replay or manipulation attacks, and correlate UWB addresses with physical identity if the RTLS system maps tag IDs to personnel records.
findings.impact: An attacker with RF capture hardware can passively map the entire UWB infrastructure, identifying every tag and anchor by EUI-64 address and building a complete topology of the deployment. This enables targeted surveillance of specific individuals by correlating tag addresses to personnel assignments, preparation for sophisticated replay or distance-reduction attacks using captured ranging parameters, and identification of high-value anchors whose compromise would have maximum impact on system integrity.
findings.remediation_brief: Configure all UWB devices to operate in IEEE 802.15.4z SP3 mode with STS enabled to provide authenticated timestamps and prevent frame-level eavesdropping of the ranging exchange metadata. Where SP3 is not available on legacy hardware, enable application-layer payload encryption and minimise identifying information in ranging frame payloads. Segment UWB traffic to the minimum required RF coverage area and use directional antennas to reduce unintended RF leakage beyond the operational boundary.

findings.title: Wireless Vulnerability: RTLS Anchor Firmware Update Without Signature Verification
findings.description: The RTLS anchor firmware update mechanism accepts firmware images submitted via the management API or a dedicated OTA update endpoint without cryptographically verifying the image signature against a vendor-controlled public key. An attacker with network access to the RTLS management interface and low-privilege credentials (or no credentials if the API is unauthenticated) can submit a crafted firmware image to any or all anchors, replacing the legitimate firmware with a malicious version that modifies ranging behaviour, exfiltrates UWB frame data, disrupts positioning, or establishes persistent backdoor access to anchor hardware. Because anchors run continuously and are often physically inaccessible, compromised firmware may persist undetected for extended periods.
findings.impact: An attacker can replace anchor firmware with a malicious version, achieving persistent hardware-level compromise of the RTLS infrastructure. Compromised anchors can silently manipulate ranging calculations to produce false position data, exfiltrate sensitive UWB frame data to attacker-controlled endpoints, serve as a persistent network foothold, and resist remediation since anchors are typically in physically inaccessible ceiling or wall-mounted locations. A fleet-wide firmware compromise could render the entire RTLS system untrustworthy and require physical replacement of all anchor hardware.
findings.remediation_brief: Implement mandatory cryptographic signature verification on all firmware images prior to installation; the verification key should be stored in anchor hardware (e.g., a one-time-programmable fuse or secure element) and should not be overridable via software. Require HTTPS and strong API authentication for all firmware update endpoints. Implement a firmware version manifest with expected hash values that the anchor compares against the received image before flashing. Add firmware attestation capabilities so the RTLS platform can detect unexpected firmware version changes across the anchor fleet.

mitre_attack.name: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain

findings.title: IoT: MQTT Cleartext Credential Transmission
findings.description: MQTT clients connecting to the RTLS broker transmit credentials (username and password) in cleartext over TCP port 1883 without TLS encryption. Any attacker with the ability to perform network interception — via ARP spoofing, a compromised network switch, or proximity to a wireless access point carrying the RTLS traffic — can capture CONNECT packets and extract credentials in plaintext using standard tools such as Wireshark or tshark. Captured credentials can be replayed to gain authenticated access to the MQTT broker, or may be tested against other services if credential reuse is present across the RTLS platform.
findings.impact: An attacker who intercepts MQTT traffic can extract plaintext credentials from CONNECT packets, gaining authenticated access to the broker. If credentials are shared with other RTLS platform components (management console, REST API), the attacker achieves cross-component access escalation. Captured credentials enable persistent access that survives network topology changes and can be used from any network location, unlike passive eavesdropping which requires continued positioning on the traffic path.
findings.remediation_brief: Migrate all MQTT communication to TLS-encrypted port 8883 using a certificate chain rooted in an internal CA. Disable plaintext port 1883 at the broker configuration level and ensure firewall rules block external access to it. Rotate all MQTT credentials that have been transmitted in cleartext and treat them as compromised. Implement certificate pinning on MQTT clients where supported to prevent interception via rogue CA attacks.

findings.title: Authentication Bypass: RTLS Zone Boundary Bypass
findings.description: By combining the Ghost Peak distance reduction technique (AETHU-001) with knowledge of zone boundary geometry extracted from the RTLS management API (AETHU-006), an attacker can manipulate the measured distances between a tag and surrounding anchors in a coordinated manner such that the RTLS location engine calculates a tag position inside an authorised zone while the tag carrier is physically located outside of it. This zone spoofing attack allows an attacker to trigger zone-entry events without physical presence in the zone, bypass zone-based access control logic (e.g., automated door unlocking triggered by zone occupancy), and disable zone-exit alerts for personnel who have physically departed a restricted area.
findings.impact: An attacker can defeat zone-based physical access controls and safety systems by manipulating UWB ranging to place a tag inside a zone it has not physically entered. This enables unauthorized entry through UWB-triggered automated doors, suppression of restricted-area departure alerts allowing unauthorized prolonged access, triggering of false zone-entry events to create confusion or distraction, and systematic undermining of geofence-based safety interlocks in hazardous industrial environments.
findings.remediation_brief: Implement multi-anchor consistency checks that flag ranging results where the set of anchor distances does not geometrically converge within an expected error bound; anomalous trilateration inputs should trigger an alert rather than producing a position estimate. Augment UWB-based zone enforcement with complementary access control mechanisms (e.g., badge readers, PIN pads, or video verification) that must all confirm authorisation independently. Enable STS mode on all anchors to mitigate the underlying Ghost Peak attack vector. Define conservative zone boundaries with a safety margin that accounts for the maximum expected ranging error.

findings.title: UWB: Anchor RF Flooding / Denial of Service
findings.description: The UWB channel used by the RTLS anchors can be saturated with high-rate UWB pulse transmissions from an attacker-controlled RF source (e.g., a custom firmware DWM3000EVB or SDR with UWB frontend), preventing legitimate ranging exchanges from completing and causing the RTLS system to lose position data for all tags within the affected coverage area. During a DoS condition the RTLS engine reports tags as lost or stationary at their last known position, which can disable safety alarms, automated zone logic, and personnel tracking. This finding requires physical proximity to the target environment and the use of appropriate RF transmission equipment. NOTE: This test requires explicit dos_authorized=true in the configuration and appropriate RF authorisation from the client.
findings.impact: An attacker can deny positioning service to the entire RTLS deployment or a targeted coverage zone by flooding the UWB channel, causing all tags to report as lost or frozen at stale positions. This disables real-time personnel safety monitoring, zone-based automated access controls, asset tracking, and any business process that depends on continuous position updates. In safety-critical environments such as mining, construction, or healthcare, loss of personnel tracking during an emergency creates direct life-safety risk.
findings.remediation_brief: Deploy UWB hardware that supports channel agility and can automatically switch to an alternative UWB channel (as defined in IEEE 802.15.4z) when interference is detected. Implement RTLS application-level monitoring that alerts operators when anchor-to-tag ranging failure rates exceed a threshold, indicating potential RF interference or DoS. Define an operational procedure for switching to a backup positioning method (Wi-Fi RTT, BLE triangulation) if UWB becomes unavailable. Physically secure the RF environment by using appropriate shielding and minimising UWB signal leakage beyond the operational perimeter.

findings.title: Injection: RTLS Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) in Dashboard
findings.description: The RTLS web dashboard reflects tag label values and custom metadata fields into the HTML page without adequate output encoding, enabling stored cross-site scripting attacks. An attacker who can write a tag label (via the management API or by injecting data through the MQTT broker) can insert a malicious script payload that executes in the browser of any RTLS operator who views the dashboard or tag detail page. Successful XSS enables session cookie theft, credential harvesting via overlay login forms, lateral movement to other web applications accessible from the operator's browser, and persistent dashboard manipulation that misleads operators about system state.
findings.impact: An attacker can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the browser of any RTLS administrator or operator who views the dashboard, enabling session hijacking, credential theft via phishing overlays, exfiltration of displayed position data, and persistent manipulation of the dashboard display to hide attacker activity. Because the XSS payload is stored in the database via tag labels, it persists across sessions and affects every user who views the compromised tag, creating a wormable attack vector across the entire operator team.
findings.remediation_brief: Apply strict HTML output encoding (using a context-aware escaping library such as OWASP Java Encoder or equivalent) to all dynamic values rendered in the dashboard, including tag labels, zone names, anchor aliases, and custom metadata fields. Implement a Content Security Policy (CSP) header that disallows inline scripts and restricts script sources to the application's own origin. Sanitise all API-sourced string fields before storage using an allowlist of permitted characters appropriate to the field type (e.g., alphanumeric plus limited punctuation for tag labels).

findings.title: Broken Access Control: Insecure Direct Object Reference in RTLS API
findings.description: The RTLS REST API uses sequential integer or predictable UUID identifiers for sensor records, tags, and user accounts, and does not enforce ownership or role checks when these identifiers are accessed by authenticated but low-privilege users. An attacker with any valid API credential can iterate over sensor IDs, tag IDs, and user profile IDs to retrieve configuration and location data belonging to other RTLS users or system components. In multi-tenant RTLS deployments this constitutes a cross-tenant data breach; in single-tenant deployments it allows a low-privilege operator to access administrator-level sensor configurations and historical position records without the required privilege level.
findings.impact: An attacker with low-privilege credentials can enumerate and access all records in the RTLS system by iterating over predictable identifiers, including other users' profiles and credentials, administrator-level sensor configurations, tag assignment records linking tag IDs to tracked individuals, and historical position data for any tracked entity. In multi-tenant deployments this constitutes a cross-tenant data breach exposing one customer's location data to another.
findings.remediation_brief: Implement server-side authorisation checks on every API endpoint that accesses an object by ID, validating that the authenticated user has the required role or ownership relationship to access the requested object. Use cryptographically random UUIDs instead of sequential integers for resource identifiers to eliminate predictable enumeration, while recognising that random IDs are a defence-in-depth measure and not a substitute for proper authorisation logic. Conduct a full audit of RTLS API routes against the intended access control matrix.

findings.title: UWB: Physical UWB Frame Injection
findings.description: An attacker with physical access to the RF environment and an RF injection-capable device (e.g., a second DWM3000EVB with custom firmware, or a Software Defined Radio with UWB-capable frontend) can transmit forged IEEE 802.15.4z frames that impersonate legitimate anchors, injecting false ranging responses into the Two-Way Ranging exchange. When the RTLS engine processes ranging results that include injected forged anchor responses alongside legitimate ones, the trilateration calculation produces a position estimate displaced from the tag's true location. This attack can be used to systematically move perceived tag positions into or out of authorised zones, generate false alarms, or mask the movement of assets through restricted areas. This finding requires physical_access and injection_authorized to be enabled in the configuration. NOTE: Full execution requires specialised hardware operating under explicit RF testing authorisation.
findings.impact: An attacker can displace the calculated position of any tracked tag by injecting forged ranging responses from impersonated anchors, causing the RTLS engine to produce incorrect position estimates. This enables systematic movement of perceived tag positions across zone boundaries to defeat access controls, generation of false zone-entry alarms to overwhelm operators and desensitize monitoring, masking of actual asset or personnel movements through restricted areas, and long-term degradation of RTLS positioning accuracy that erodes operator trust in the system.
findings.remediation_brief: Enable IEEE 802.15.4z STS (SP3 mode) on all anchors and tags to cryptographically authenticate ranging frame timestamps; forged frames without the correct STS cannot produce consistent time-of-flight measurements that pass integrity checks. Implement anchor-to-anchor cross-validation where each anchor computes expected ranging windows for neighbouring anchors and flags unexpected ranging responses from unknown sources. Deploy RF anomaly detection that identifies transmission power levels, pulse repetition frequencies, or ranging schedules inconsistent with the commissioned anchor configuration. Physically secure anchor hardware to prevent tampering with antenna orientation or co-location of rogue devices.

findings.title: MQTT Cleartext Credential Transmission
findings.description: The MQTT broker accepts client connections on port 1883 (cleartext TCP) and transmits authentication credentials without TLS encryption. The MQTT CONNECT packet carries the username and password fields in plaintext, which are visible to any network observer positioned between the client and broker. Standard network sniffing tools such as Wireshark, tshark, or tcpdump can extract these credentials with trivial effort. This affects all MQTT clients connecting to the RTLS platform including tag gateways, anchor management agents, and the management console's MQTT integration, meaning a single interception point exposes credentials for multiple system components.
findings.impact: Credentials transmitted in cleartext are visible to any attacker with network sniffing capability on the same segment, enabling complete MQTT broker takeover. Once MQTT credentials are captured, the attacker can subscribe to all position data topics for real-time surveillance, publish fabricated position data to manipulate RTLS operations, and test captured credentials against other platform components where credential reuse is common in RTLS deployments.
findings.remediation_brief: Migrate all MQTT communication to port 8883 with mandatory TLS encryption using certificates signed by the organization's internal CA. Disable the plaintext listener on port 1883 entirely at the broker configuration level. Rotate all MQTT credentials that have ever been transmitted over cleartext port 1883 as they should be considered compromised. Enforce TLS 1.2 or higher with strong cipher suites on the encrypted listener.

findings.title: MQTT Topic ACL Bypass
findings.description: The MQTT broker allows authenticated clients to publish messages to restricted administrative and configuration topics without enforcing topic-level Access Control Lists (ACLs). An attacker with any valid MQTT credential — even one provisioned for read-only position data subscription — can publish arbitrary payloads to administrative topics such as $SYS/broker/config, admin/anchors/config, or platform-specific management channels. This effectively elevates any authenticated MQTT session to full administrative control over the RTLS configuration via the MQTT interface, bypassing the role-based access controls implemented in the web management console.
findings.impact: An attacker with low-privilege MQTT credentials can reconfigure the entire RTLS system by publishing to unrestricted admin topics, including modifying anchor placements and zone boundaries, changing broker configuration parameters, injecting false position data by publishing to position update topics, and silently disabling geofence alerts by altering zone definition topics. This privilege escalation bypasses all web console access controls since the changes are made directly via the MQTT data plane.
findings.remediation_brief: Implement per-topic ACL rules on the MQTT broker that restrict publish and subscribe operations based on client identity. In Mosquitto use mosquitto_acl_file or the dynamic security plugin; in EMQX use the built-in ACL module. Follow least privilege: position data consumers should have subscribe-only access to position topics, and configuration topics should be writable only by the management console service account. Test ACL enforcement by attempting restricted publishes with low-privilege credentials.

findings.title: Missing CSRF Protection on RTLS API
findings.description: State-changing API endpoints on the RTLS management console — including configuration updates, user account creation, firmware upload triggers, and zone boundary modifications — do not implement Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) protection tokens. Requests are authenticated solely by session cookies, which browsers attach automatically to cross-origin requests. An attacker who lures an authenticated RTLS administrator to a malicious web page can silently submit forged POST/PUT/DELETE requests to the management console using the administrator's active session, executing privileged operations without the administrator's knowledge or consent.
findings.impact: A malicious web page visited by an authenticated RTLS administrator can silently modify RTLS configuration, create backdoor user accounts, change zone boundaries to disable safety alerts, push firmware updates, or exfiltrate configuration data. The attack requires only that the administrator visit an attacker-controlled page while logged into the management console, which can be accomplished via phishing or by compromising a frequently visited website. All forged actions execute with the administrator's full privileges.
findings.remediation_brief: Implement synchronizer token pattern or double-submit cookie CSRF protection on all state-changing endpoints. Set the SameSite cookie attribute to Strict or Lax on all session cookies. Validate the Origin and Referer headers on POST, PUT, and DELETE requests. If the management console uses a JavaScript SPA, generate a CSRF token on login and include it as a custom header (e.g., X-CSRF-Token) in every mutating API request.

findings.title: No Account Lockout or Rate Limiting
findings.description: The RTLS management console authentication endpoint does not implement account lockout, progressive delay, or IP-based rate limiting. An attacker can submit an unlimited number of login attempts at maximum speed without triggering any defensive response. Testing confirmed that 15 or more consecutive failed authentication attempts against the same account produced no lockout, no CAPTCHA challenge, and no observable throttling. This enables online brute-force attacks and credential-stuffing campaigns against the management console at speeds limited only by network latency.
findings.impact: The absence of lockout or rate limiting enables attackers to conduct high-speed brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks against the RTLS management console. Given that many RTLS deployments use short passwords or factory-adjacent credentials, the time to recover valid credentials is significantly reduced. A successful brute-force attack grants full administrative control over the RTLS infrastructure, including the ability to reconfigure anchors, extract all position data, and modify zone boundaries.
findings.remediation_brief: Implement progressive account lockout that temporarily locks an account after 5 consecutive failed login attempts with exponential backoff (30 seconds, 2 minutes, 15 minutes). Apply IP-based rate limiting on authentication endpoints (e.g., 10 requests per minute per source IP) using the web server configuration or a reverse proxy. Log all failed authentication attempts with source IP and timestamp for security monitoring. Consider implementing CAPTCHA after 3 failed attempts where the platform supports it.

findings.title: Missing Security Response Headers
findings.description: The RTLS management console HTTP responses are missing one or more recommended security headers: Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS), Content-Security-Policy (CSP), X-Frame-Options, and X-Content-Type-Options. Missing HSTS allows SSL-stripping downgrade attacks against administrators who navigate to the console via HTTP. Missing CSP increases the exploitability of any XSS vulnerability by allowing inline script execution and unrestricted external resource loading. Missing X-Frame-Options enables clickjacking attacks where the management console is embedded in a malicious iframe to trick administrators into performing unintended actions. Missing X-Content-Type-Options allows MIME-type confusion attacks.
findings.impact: The absence of security headers increases the attack surface for browser-based attacks against RTLS operators. Specifically, missing HSTS enables SSL-stripping man-in-the-middle attacks to intercept administrator sessions; missing CSP amplifies the impact of any XSS vulnerability by removing script execution restrictions; missing X-Frame-Options enables clickjacking where administrators are tricked into clicking concealed management console buttons; and missing X-Content-Type-Options may allow script injection via MIME confusion.
findings.remediation_brief: Configure the RTLS web server to return the following headers on all responses: Strict-Transport-Security with max-age of at least 31536000 and includeSubDomains; Content-Security-Policy that restricts script sources to self and whitelisted CDNs; X-Frame-Options set to DENY or SAMEORIGIN; X-Content-Type-Options set to nosniff. If the RTLS platform does not support custom header configuration, deploy a reverse proxy (nginx, Apache, HAProxy) in front of the management console to inject these headers.

findings.title: Permissive CORS Configuration
findings.description: The RTLS API endpoints return an overly permissive Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, either set to wildcard (*) or dynamically reflecting the request's Origin header without validation against an allowlist. When combined with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, this allows any web page on the internet to make authenticated cross-origin requests to the RTLS API and read the responses using the victim's active session cookie. An attacker can host a malicious page that silently exfiltrates real-time position data, sensor configurations, user details, and zone definitions from the RTLS platform when visited by an authenticated operator.
findings.impact: Cross-origin JavaScript from any attacker-controlled website can read authenticated RTLS API responses and submit state-changing requests when an RTLS operator visits the attacker's page. This enables silent exfiltration of real-time position data for all tracked entities, extraction of anchor and zone configurations, modification of RTLS settings via cross-origin PUT/POST requests, and creation of persistent backdoor accounts through the API, all without requiring the attacker to have any direct network access to the RTLS infrastructure.
findings.remediation_brief: Configure CORS to allow only the specific origin(s) that legitimately need cross-origin access to the RTLS API (typically just the management console's own origin). Never reflect the Origin header as Access-Control-Allow-Origin without checking it against a strict whitelist. Set Access-Control-Allow-Credentials to false unless cross-origin cookie-based authentication is genuinely required. If the API is intended for same-origin use only, remove all CORS headers entirely.

findings.title: Insecure Session Cookie Flags
findings.description: Session cookies issued by the RTLS management console are missing one or more critical security flags. Missing HttpOnly allows JavaScript access to session tokens via document.cookie, enabling XSS-based session theft. Missing Secure allows session cookies to be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections, exposing them to network interception. Missing SameSite allows session cookies to be sent with cross-site requests, weakening CSRF defences. Testing confirmed that the session cookie lacks at least one of these flags, creating multiple exploitation vectors that compound other vulnerabilities in the RTLS management console.
findings.impact: Session tokens are exposed to theft through multiple vectors: any XSS vulnerability (including AETHU-013) can exfiltrate the session cookie via document.cookie due to missing HttpOnly; a network attacker can capture session tokens transmitted over HTTP due to missing Secure flag; and CSRF attacks (AETHU-018) are facilitated by missing SameSite restrictions. Stolen session tokens enable full impersonation of the victim administrator with complete control over the RTLS platform.
findings.remediation_brief: Set HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite=Strict (or Lax) flags on all session cookies. Ensure the management console is served exclusively over HTTPS so the Secure flag does not break functionality. If the platform's session management does not support these flags natively, configure them at the reverse proxy layer using header-rewriting rules (e.g., nginx proxy_cookie_flags directive). Verify the changes by inspecting Set-Cookie headers in the HTTP response.

findings.title: MQTT TLS Not Available
findings.description: Port 8883 (MQTT over TLS) is not open on the MQTT broker host, meaning no encrypted MQTT transport option is available for RTLS clients. All MQTT communication — including authentication credentials, real-time position data streams, zone event notifications, and administrative commands — must traverse the network in cleartext on port 1883. Unlike findings where TLS exists but is not enforced, this indicates that TLS-encrypted MQTT is entirely unavailable as a deployment option, making cleartext the only protocol path for all MQTT traffic in the RTLS platform.
findings.impact: All MQTT traffic in the RTLS deployment is unencrypted with no option for TLS protection, meaning every credential exchange, every real-time position update, every zone event, and every administrative command is visible to network observers. This exposes the complete operational state of the RTLS system to passive interception. In environments where RTLS tracks personnel for safety or security purposes, the inability to encrypt position data creates a systemic privacy and safety risk that cannot be mitigated without infrastructure changes.
findings.remediation_brief: Enable TLS on the MQTT broker by generating or obtaining a server certificate and configuring the broker to listen on port 8883 with TLS enabled. For Mosquitto, add listener 8883, cafile, certfile, and keyfile directives to mosquitto.conf. For EMQX, configure the SSL listener in emqx.conf. After enabling port 8883, migrate all RTLS clients to the TLS-encrypted port and then disable the cleartext 1883 listener entirely.

findings.title: Position Data Export Exposure
findings.description: The RTLS management console exposes position history export and bulk data download endpoints that return large volumes of historical location data with insufficient access controls. These endpoints allow retrieval of complete movement histories for all tracked tags and personnel, including timestamps, coordinates, zone transitions, and dwell times. The export functionality is either unauthenticated or accessible to low-privilege users who should not have access to bulk historical data. In deployments where tags are assigned to individuals, this data constitutes personally identifiable information (PII) revealing detailed movement patterns, work schedules, break habits, and interpersonal interactions.
findings.impact: An attacker can download comprehensive historical movement data for every tracked individual and asset, enabling pattern-of-life analysis that reveals daily routines, frequently visited locations, social connections, and schedule deviations. In healthcare environments, this exposes patient movement patterns protected under HIPAA. In industrial settings, it reveals operational workflows and personnel allocation. In defense or government deployments, it provides intelligence-grade surveillance data. The bulk export capability means a single unauthorized access event yields the complete historical dataset rather than just a point-in-time snapshot.
findings.remediation_brief: Require explicit administrative authentication and authorization for all data export endpoints. Implement role-based access control that restricts bulk export to designated data administrators. Add rate limiting on export operations (maximum 1 export per minute per user). Implement comprehensive audit logging for every export request including the requesting user, timestamp, and data range. Consider implementing data retention policies that automatically purge position history older than operational requirements. In regulated environments, encrypt exported data and require MFA before allowing bulk downloads.

findings.title: JWT Algorithm None Accepted
findings.description: The RTLS management console's JWT validation implementation accepts tokens with the 'alg' header field set to 'none', meaning the server trusts tokens with no cryptographic signature. An attacker can craft a JWT with arbitrary claims — including administrator role claims, any user identity, and any custom permissions — append an empty signature segment, and the server accepts it as a legitimately signed token. This is a complete authentication and authorization bypass that requires no knowledge of the signing key, no brute-force effort, and no social engineering. The 'alg: none' vulnerability is a well-documented critical JWT implementation flaw referenced by CVE-2015-9235.
findings.impact: An attacker can forge any JWT claim including administrator privileges, gaining complete unauthenticated administrative access to the RTLS management console. This enables full control over the RTLS infrastructure: reconfiguring anchors, modifying zones, extracting all position data, creating persistent backdoor accounts, pushing firmware updates, and accessing all API endpoints without restriction. Because the bypass requires no credentials or prior access, any network-reachable attacker can achieve immediate full administrative compromise of the entire RTLS platform.
findings.remediation_brief: Configure the JWT validation library to reject tokens with alg=none unconditionally. Use an explicit allowlist of accepted algorithms (e.g., only RS256 or ES256) and never trust the alg header from the token itself to select the validation algorithm. Upgrade the JWT library to a current version that rejects alg=none by default. If using a framework-level JWT middleware, verify that the 'algorithms' parameter is explicitly set. After patching, rotate all signing keys as a precaution and invalidate all existing sessions to force re-authentication.
